paragraphs: Worth trying first: willing to stand continuously under the equipment takt and fit punches and dies, load material and monitor by hand, able to set the stroke, stops and speed to work orders and drawings and verify the first piece with measuring tools, willing to follow die locking, guards and interlocks and energy isolation procedures strictly, and stopping the machine before reporting when there is an abnormal sound, die misalignment or dimensional deviation.

Consider carefully: if you find it hard to adapt to equipment takt and repetitive motions, are sensitive to a noisy and oily environment, are unwilling to measure and verify repeatedly, or find die locking and stopping and tagging procedures troublesome, the actual work will differ from your expectations.

The core output is punching and shearing results that meet specification and can be traced, together with records: workpieces cut or formed to specification, first-piece and sampling measurement records, die fitting and stroke setting records, non-conforming item sorting and equipment readjustment records, run data and output records, and equipment cleaning and lubrication records — not "how many parts you punched".

Low-risk validation: using safe materials such as card or thin plastic sheet, complete one exercise — "read the dimensions and tolerances from a fictional work order — write a die and stroke setting card — draw up a first-piece measurement and sorting table — write out the stop-and-report process for die misalignment and a guard or interlock anomaly" — this only assesses work preferences; the exercise does not operate real running punching or shearing equipment or involve real production orders, and is not equivalent to employer hiring or equipment operation authorization.

Judgment focus: whether, under the constraints of work order tolerances, die and equipment takt and machine safety procedures, you can turn die fitting and stroke setting, loading and monitoring, measurement and sorting and deburring into machining records that are verifiable, transferable and traceable.

Work pace is set by the stroke takt of the punching or shearing press, and one person often has to tend one or more machines and change dies frequently as orders and dies change; across metal sheet and plastic parts, equipment types, dies and inspection standards differ markedly.

Similar job titles among adjacent occupations do not mean the same duties; when comparing, first look at whether the focus is punching and shearing equipment, cutting and slicing machines, forging equipment, grinding and polishing machine tools, milling and planing machine tools, multiple machine tools, or tool and die making and sharpening, and whether the role carries die fitting, stroke setting or quality release responsibility.

Work orders, drawings, die drawings and measuring tool readings may be treated as inputs that must be verified, but you must not skip die locking and stroke verification and first-piece measurement based on experience, nor keep running when a guard or interlock is abnormal on the basis of "finish punching first".
A fit assessment should be checked against real work observation, mentoring feedback and your own condition; it cannot be replaced by an interest type or a single test.

All paper exercises on this page use fictional materials; in real production, equipment operation, die mounting, removal and locking, guard and interlock checks, energy isolation, personal protection and finished goods inspection must follow machine safety procedures, work instructions and employer policies.

The work of metal punching and shearing equipment operation can be divided into three connected but distinct work areas. The first is die fitting and machine setup: reading the work order or production schedule to determine the material, cutting line position, dimensions and tolerances; using gauges, templates, feeler gauges, shims and hand tools to fit, align and lock punches, dies, blades and fixtures on the ram or machine table; adjusting the stroke length to specification, setting the positions of stops, guides and support blocks, and turning controls to set the cutting speed, feed rate or table angle. The second is loading and monitoring the run: placing and aligning the workpiece on the cutting table or die by hand or with lifting gear, cranes and skids; loading and feeding workpieces, plastic material or chemical solutions into the machine; turning on coolant or chip-blowing air, starting the machine, monitoring the run and recording run data; testing and adjusting machine speed or action with gauges and hand tools, and changing dies and adjusting the ram or press components during multiple or continuous strokes. The third is measurement, inspection and maintenance close-out: measuring finished workpieces with micrometers, gauges, calipers, templates or straightedges to verify specification, checking for defects such as notches and scratches and sorting by defect type; sharpening blunt blades with bench grinders, grinding wheels or lathes and replacing damaged blades or grinding wheels; dressing tool notches with oilstones, removing housings and feed pipes to replace worn parts such as springs or bushes; removing burrs and sharp edges with portable grinders, high-speed lathes or polishing stands, joining sheet metal parts with equipment such as spot welders, and cleaning and lubricating the machine and tidying the workstation. The three work areas alternate, but their basis, risk and responsibility differ; so do the equipment, parameters and inspection standards for different materials and die types.

This occupation shares some setting and inspection tasks with forging, grinding, milling and planing and multiple machine tools, but grinding, milling and planing are not as a rule press working. Forging includes cold and hot processes and tasks such as cutting and punching, and this occupation also lists preheating, so an absolute boundary cannot be drawn on whether heat is used. Multiple machine tools means more than one kind of machine or robot and does not necessarily mean tending several at once.
Core purpose
Set up, operate or tend machines to saw, cut, shear, slit, punch, crimp, notch, bend or straighten metal or plastic material so that workpiece dimensions and shapes meet the drawings and tolerances.

Adjacent occupations are mainly cold and hot forging forming, grinding and polishing, milling and planing, and operating more than one kind of cutting or forming machine; they share inspection and setting but the processes differ.
Main objects and basis

Metal or plastic sheet and workpieces, punches and dies, blades and fixtures, work orders and die drawings; the basis is drawing dimensions and tolerances, die and equipment parameters, machine safety procedures, and the employer's review and escalation paths.

Verified by forging material and equipment, abrasive surface standards, milling and planing tools and fixturing, and multiple machine tool types; it is not a blanket distinction by number of machines or whether heat is used.
Core process
Read the work order and drawing → fit and lock the dies and adjust the stroke → load and monitor the run → measure, inspect and sort → sharpen or replace tools → deburr and clean up.

Adjacent work may be cold or hot forging, clamping and grinding, tool setting and milling and planing, or operating several kinds of machine tools in sequence; the actual process may include overlap such as cutting, punching and trimming.
Main outputs

Punched and sheared parts meeting dimensions and tolerances, first-piece and sampling measurement records, die fitting and stroke setting records, non-conforming item sorting records, run data and output records.

Outputs are verified against the actual specifications of forgings, ground parts, milled and planed parts or multi-process workpieces, and multiple machine tool output is not uniformly called assembled parts.
Responsible party

Staff in this occupation are responsible for the dimensions, shapes and sorting results of their own batches; die mounting, removal and locking, stroke setting, guard and interlock checks and energy isolation must follow machine safety procedures and employer policies, not their unilateral decision.
Each position's safety, quality, maintenance and release authority follows employer policy, and the occupation title does not confer final decision authority.
Collaboration and supervision

Collaborate with workers in the same process, inspectors, die and repair staff and team leaders within the scope of authority, and report to a supervisor or along the review path; when a die is misaligned or loose, a guard or interlock fails, there is an abnormal sound, material jams or dimensions are out of tolerance, stop the machine, isolate and report, refer and keep records according to procedure.

Adjacent staff's inspection, die, repair and process collaboration is verified against the actual employer; the names of cold and hot forging, grinding, milling and planing and multiple machine tools do not imply a uniform programming or heating position configuration.
Boundary of conclusions

Similar job titles do not mean the same duties: whether the focus is punching and shearing equipment, forging equipment, grinding wheel grinding, milling and planing machine tools, or multiple machine tools and tool and die making — and whether the role carries die fitting, stroke setting or quality release responsibility — determines the scope of duties and how performance is assessed, and the roles cannot be swapped by title.

The preparation levels and equipment operation requirements of adjacent occupations do not apply to this occupation; verify them item by item against each occupation's official materials and the requirements of the position.
Key occupational judgments

Six recurring professional judgments: whether the work order, drawing and tolerances are read correctly and the material and dies match; whether the punches, dies and blades are fitted, aligned and locked properly; whether the stroke length, stops and guides are set to specification; whether first-piece measurement and sampling are checked against the standards and defects sorted as required; whether tool and grinding wheel sharpening and replacement, machine cleaning and lubrication and equipment condition meet the requirements; and whether, when a die is misaligned or loose, a guard or interlock fails, material jams or dimensions are out of tolerance, the machine is stopped, the item isolated and the matter escalated first.
Determine the material, cutting line position, dimensions and tolerances from the work order or production schedule and verify the batch; misreading leads to whole-batch dimensional errors and scrap.

Use tools and measuring instruments to fit, align and lock the punches, dies, blades and fixtures, and use feeler gauges and shims to confirm they seat properly; improper fitting causes misalignment, jamming and die damage.
Adjust the stroke length to specification and set the stops and guides, confirming component condition during multiple or continuous strokes; incorrect setting causes deviation and equipment damage.

Measure finished workpieces with micrometers, gauges and calipers to verify specification, check for notches and scratches and sort by defect type; missed inspection or misjudgement lets out-of-tolerance parts flow into the next process.
Judgment four: Do the first-piece check and sorting follow the standards?

Sharpen or replace blades and grinding wheels according to their condition, dress notches with oilstones and clean, lubricate and check the machine; blunt tools and poor lubrication cause quality problems and equipment failure.
Judgment five: Are the tools and machine maintained properly?

On misalignment, looseness, protection failure or jamming, stop the relevant run according to procedure and report; applicable maintenance is carried out by authorized personnel who isolate hazardous energy, control stored energy and verify, and a button is not isolation.

Work context and working conditions

Different punching, shearing, pressing, sawing and bending or straightening workstations each require verification of equipment takt, stance, noise and material risk; the U.S. respondent work context on this page is not a uniform Chinese working condition or disease rate.

Among U.S. respondents, 97% using common protective equipment every day is a combined question and does not mean each person wears every item listed; 90% have daily contact with distracting or uncomfortable noise, 57% have daily contact with hazards such as minor burns and cuts, and 39% have daily contact with hazardous conditions. Hazard exposure is not the actual injury proportion, and noise frequency does not prove that a dose limit is exceeded or that hearing is damaged.

Metal and plastic workpieces and the actual punches, dies, blades, measuring tools, coolant and lifting tools are verified separately. The 31 tasks include supplementary spot welding, preheating, deburring and sharpening, and not everyone does all of them. paragraphs: Forging Machine Setters, Operators, and Tenders, Metal and Plastic (adjacent occupation, 51-4022.00)
Set up and operate forging hammers or presses to forge and finish metal at high or ambient temperature.

The difference is that the core is forging dies and hot forming, and the billet undergoes large plastic deformation; this occupation mainly does blanking, punching and bending with punching and shearing dies.
Better suited to people who want to do forging heating and forming.
Grinding, Lapping, Polishing, and Buffing Machine Tool Setters, Operators, and Tenders, Metal and Plastic (adjacent occupation, 51-4033.00)
Set up and operate grinding, polishing and chamfering machines, using grinding wheels and abrasives to machine workpiece surfaces and dimensions.

The difference is that the core is surface processing with grinding wheels and abrasives and the role is not responsible for blanking and punching; this occupation centres on punching and shearing forming, with grinding being only deburring and dressing.
Better suited to people who want to specialise in surface processing and grinding.
Milling and Planing Machine Setters, Operators, and Tenders, Metal and Plastic (adjacent occupation, 51-4035.00)
The difference is that it relies on rotating cutting tools for removal machining and is mainly single-piece or small batch; this occupation relies on dies and the stroke for punching and shearing.
Better suited to people who want to do milling and planing work.
Multiple Machine Tool Setters, Operators, and Tenders, Metal and Plastic (adjacent occupation, 51-4081.00)
The difference is that it cycles through several machine tools with a wider process span; this occupation usually tends one class of operation, punching or shearing.
Better suited to people who want to tend several machines under a demanding takt.
Tool and Die Makers (adjacent occupation, 51-4111.00)

The difference is that the core is making and repairing dies and precision tools, oriented to tooling manufacture; this occupation uses dies for batch processing and is not responsible for designing and making dies.
Better suited to people who want to do precision tooling manufacture and repair.
Tool Grinders, Filers, and Sharpeners (adjacent occupation, 51-4194.00)
The difference is that it specialises in the cutting edges and geometry of cutting tools and tools; sharpening in this occupation is only one part of equipment maintenance.
Better suited to people who want to specialise in tool sharpening and dressing.

values: Fictional production scenario material (exercise input)

Fictional scenario: a punching and shearing equipment operator encounters four problems during a shift. First, a die set was set for the previous batch of material and this batch is slightly different in thickness; second, after the trial punch the first piece's dimensions fall at the tolerance edge and the delivery date is very tight; third, an abnormal sound is heard while the equipment runs and it is unclear whether an interlock indicator on the guard is normal; fourth, one die set needs its blades changed, the maintenance worker says it will be dealt with later, and the team leader is pressing to keep producing.

Materials provided: work order dimensions and drawings; die fitting and stroke setting requirements; first-piece measurement and defect sorting requirements; guard and interlock requirements and the energy isolation and maintenance reporting procedures.

Materials not provided: the rules for judging and conceding an edge dimension, the authority to handle an abnormal sound, whether changing blades requires stopping and isolation, and the priority between servicing and production. If the exercise requires these conditions, state your assumptions and the people you need to confirm with.
Task requirements

Please write a one-page handling and reporting plan covering: die and stroke re-verification and trial punch arrangements, handling of the edge dimension, verification of the abnormal sound and guard interlock and the decision to stop, and arrangements for changing blades and servicing.

The plan must state which information comes from the given materials and which is still assumption, and indicate whether the basis is the drawing, the measurement requirements or the machine safety and energy isolation procedures.
Reference deliverable (can be derived from the prompt)

The plan should include: die and stroke re-verification (verify the die and stroke against this batch's material and trial punch again to confirm, not carrying over the previous batch's settings), an edge dimension (re-measure and verify whether it is within tolerance, and when out of tolerance or uncertain stop the machine, isolate and report according to procedure without releasing on your own), an abnormal sound and guard interlock (stop the machine first, do not bypass the interlock, verify the guard and interlock according to procedure and report, and resume only after confirming they are normal), changing blades and servicing (isolate the energy and apply the tag under the energy control procedure before working, do not treat a stop button as complete isolation, and report the servicing arrangement according to procedure and explain it to the team leader), and handover (state the status of the four items, the actions taken and the matters still to be confirmed).
The reference deliverable only lists the elements that should be included and does not require wording identical to the example; being able to explain the basis for your judgements is enough.
Boundaries and conclusions that cannot be inferred

This item only tests awareness of die and stroke verification, dimensional judgement, machine safety and energy isolation handling and anomaly escalation; it does not evaluate whether the handling of any real case is compliant, and it does not constitute a safety determination, liability determination or legal advice.

entries.answer: Set up, operate or tend machines to saw, cut, shear, slit, punch, crimp, notch, bend or straighten metal or plastic material: reading the work order or production schedule to determine the material, cutting line position, dimensions and tolerances; using gauges, templates, feeler gauges, shims and hand tools to fit, align and lock punches, dies, blades and fixtures; adjusting the stroke length and setting the positions of stops, guides and fixtures and setting the cutting speed, feed rate or table angle; placing and aligning the workpiece, loading and feeding workpieces, plastic material or chemical solutions into the machine; turning on coolant or chip-blowing air, starting the machine, monitoring the run and recording run data; measuring finished workpieces with micrometers, gauges, calipers, templates or straightedges to verify specification; checking for defects such as notches or scratches and sorting by defect type; sharpening and dressing tools with grinding wheels, oilstones or lathes and replacing damaged blades and grinding wheels; removing burrs and sharp edges with portable grinders and joining sheet metal parts with equipment such as spot welders; and cleaning and lubricating the machine and tidying the workstation.

description.text: Cutting, Punching, and Press Machine Setters, Operators, and Tenders, Metal and Plastic (O*NET-SOC 51-4031.00) set up, operate or tend machines to saw, cut, shear, slit, punch, crimp, notch, bend or straighten metal or plastic material: covering reading the work order to determine dimensions and tolerances, fitting, aligning and locking punches, dies and blades, adjusting the stroke and stops, setting speed, feed and table angle, loading and aligning workpieces, monitoring the run and recording data, measurement inspection and sorting, sharpening and replacing tools, cleaning and lubricating the machine, and deburring sharp edges and spot welding sheet metal parts; it should be noted that its U.S. wage and employment follow this subcategory's own basis (2025 median annual wage 46,330 dollars, hourly 22.27 dollars; about 174,700 people employed in 2024; a 2024—2034 projection of a decline of -1% or lower; about 14,400 annual average openings including growth and replacement; industry distribution manufacturing 89% | other industries 11%; interest code RC), together with the industry-level gap for such positions in mainland China and control points for die locking, guards and interlocks, stroke and stop verification and first-piece measurement and deburring.

subject.name: Cutting, Punching, and Press Machine Setters, Operators, and Tenders, Metal and Plastic
subject.summary: In the United States, cutting, punching and press machine setters, operators and tenders, metal and plastic, correspond to O*NET-SOC 51-4031.00 (Cutting, Punching, and Press Machine Setters, Operators, and Tenders, Metal and Plastic), setting up, operating or tending machines to saw, cut, shear, slit, punch, crimp, notch, bend or straighten metal or plastic material: reading the work order or production schedule to determine the material, cutting line position, dimensions and tolerances; measuring finished products with micrometers, gauges, calipers, templates or straightedges to verify specification, and checking for defects such as notches and scratches and sorting by defect type; using tools and measuring instruments to fit, align and lock punches, dies, blades and fixtures and adjusting the stroke length and guide stops; setting the cutting speed, feed rate or table angle to specification, starting the machine, monitoring the run and recording run data; placing and aligning the workpiece, loading, turning on coolant or chip-blowing air, and sharpening tools and replacing blades or grinding wheels and cleaning and lubricating the machine when necessary; and removing burrs or sharp edges with grinders and joining sheet metal parts with equipment such as spot welders. The preparation level for this occupation is Job Zone 1-2 (little to some preparation, SVP below 6.0), and official education feedback shows that among new entrants 63% require a high school diploma or equivalent, 35% a postsecondary certificate and 1% less than high school, with on-the-job training ranging from a few days to a year. Comparable positions in China are punching, shearing and sheet metal forming equipment operation positions in manufacturing and processing enterprises; their duties and pay basis do not correspond one-to-one with this U.S. occupational subcategory and cannot be interchanged.
